Why would retailers create unnecessary confusion at their shops?  Not their circus, not their monkey. 
Consumers will end up paying more for everything even when dealing in cash.

In my hometown, sanitation workers clean the roads, dump the waste into the sewage right in front of us, monsoon comes, drains clog and roads flood. Then they clean the sewage, dump that sludge back onto the road, half of it washes right back in, and the rest gets picked up a week later. Then repeat. 🤦🏻

The bigger problem is that India has historically dumped sanitation work onto one community—Valmiki Samaj—and decided it's somehow “their work.” So we stigmatize the job, have a shortage of workers, overwork the ones we have, give them inadequate systems, and then blame them when the system fails.

In many Western countries, sanitation is simply a job. Here, we've turned it into a caste-assigned responsibility.

Until we stop looking down on sanitation work and start treating it as essential work that anyone can do with dignity, decent pay and proper infrastructure, we'll keep cleaning the same garbage twice and wondering why our cities are still filthy.

Subject: Story Pitch: Condition of Medical Students & Junior Doctors in Madhya Pradesh (MGM Medical College, Indore)

Dear Mr. Sarthak Goswami,

I hope this email finds you well.

I am writing to bring to your attention a matter of significant public interest concerning the condition of medical students and junior doctors across Madhya Pradesh, and to request that your desk consider covering it.

I am currently a first-year MBBS student at MGM Medical College, Indore, which is one of the highest-ranked medical colleges in the state. Based on my own experience and documentary evidence, I would like to highlight the following issues:

1. 'Vachan Patra' (Proforma-9) — Coerced Undertaking Silencing Students: As a precondition for admission, every MBBS/BDS student in Madhya Pradesh is forced to sign a notarized affidavit on Rs. 200 stamp paper stating that they are satisfied with the government-fixed course fee and monthly stipend, will never remain absent without authorization, and will never participate in any strike — under any circumstance. The document explicitly warns that if a student is found violating this clause, their admission will be cancelled under Rule 17(3) of the MP Medical Education Admission Rules, 2018. In effect, an 18-year-old is made to sign away their constitutional right to protest and their right to collectively bargain for fair stipends, under direct threat of losing their medical seat — before they have even attended their first class. I have enclosed a copy of this affidavit for your reference.

2. RURAL SERVICE BOND — One-Year Bonded Labour Clause: A separate undertaking,   RURAL SERVICE BOND  , effectively binds students/interns to a designated hospital or institution for a period of one year, denying them the freedom to choose a hospital or institution offering better pay, training, or working conditions during that period. This amounts to a de facto bonded-labour arrangement, forcing young doctors into low-paid or exploitative postings with no contractual leverage or exit option, even when better-compensated opportunities are available elsewhere.

3. Protest at GMC Bhopal: Junior doctors protesting at Gandhi Medical College (GMC), Bhopal were subjected to a lathi charge and water cannons by the police, raising serious concerns about how legitimate grievances of medical professionals are being handled by the administration — grievances that students are, on paper, not even permitted to raise.

4. Condition of Junior Doctors and Interns: Junior doctors and interns across various government hospitals in Madhya Pradesh continue to work under difficult conditions, including long duty hours, inadequate stipends, and insufficient institutional support.

5. Hostel Conditions at Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Block-2, MGMC Indore: The hostel block allotted to first-year MBBS students is reportedly in poor condition, raising safety and living-standard concerns — especially significant in light of the recent Satya Niketan, Delhi incident, which has brought student housing safety into national focus.

Taken together, these five issues point to a systemic pattern: medical students and junior doctors in Madhya Pradesh are being denied basic rights of protest, mobility, and dignified living conditions, often under the threat of losing their admission or career. I believe this story deserves wider attention, as it directly concerns the wellbeing, rights, and safety of the people who form the backbone of our healthcare system. I would be happy to share further documentation, photographs, or put you in touch with fellow students and junior doctors willing to speak on record or on condition of anonymity.

Please let me know if you would like to discuss this further or require any additional information.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Subject: Story Pitch: Condition of Medical Students & Junior Doctors in Madhya Pradesh (MGM Medical College, Indore)

Dear Mr. Sarthak Goswami,

I hope this email finds you well.

I am writing to bring to your attention a matter of significant public interest concerning the condition of medical students and junior doctors across Madhya Pradesh, and to request that your desk consider covering it.

I am currently a first-year MBBS student at MGM Medical College, Indore, which is one of the highest-ranked medical colleges in the state. Based on my own experience and documentary evidence, I would like to highlight the following issues:

1. 'Vachan Patra' (Proforma-9) — Coerced Undertaking Silencing Students: As a precondition for admission, every MBBS/BDS student in Madhya Pradesh is forced to sign a notarized affidavit on Rs. 200 stamp paper stating that they are satisfied with the government-fixed course fee and monthly stipend, will never remain absent without authorization, and will never participate in any strike — under any circumstance. The document explicitly warns that if a student is found violating this clause, their admission will be cancelled under Rule 17(3) of the MP Medical Education Admission Rules, 2018. In effect, an 18-year-old is made to sign away their constitutional right to protest and their right to collectively bargain for fair stipends, under direct threat of losing their medical seat — before they have even attended their first class. I have enclosed a copy of this affidavit for your reference.

2. RURAL SERVICE BOND — One-Year Bonded Labour Clause: A separate undertaking,   RURAL SERVICE BOND  , effectively binds students/interns to a designated hospital or institution for a period of one year, denying them the freedom to choose a hospital or institution offering better pay, training, or working conditions during that period. This amounts to a de facto bonded-labour arrangement, forcing young doctors into low-paid or exploitative postings with no contractual leverage or exit option, even when better-compensated opportunities are available elsewhere.

3. Protest at GMC Bhopal: Junior doctors protesting at Gandhi Medical College (GMC), Bhopal were subjected to a lathi charge and water cannons by the police, raising serious concerns about how legitimate grievances of medical professionals are being handled by the administration — grievances that students are, on paper, not even permitted to raise.

4. Condition of Junior Doctors and Interns: Junior doctors and interns across various government hospitals in Madhya Pradesh continue to work under difficult conditions, including long duty hours, inadequate stipends, and insufficient institutional support.

5. Hostel Conditions at Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Block-2, MGMC Indore: The hostel block allotted to first-year MBBS students is reportedly in poor condition, raising safety and living-standard concerns — especially significant in light of the recent Satya Niketan, Delhi incident, which has brought student housing safety into national focus.

Taken together, these five issues point to a systemic pattern: medical students and junior doctors in Madhya Pradesh are being denied basic rights of protest, mobility, and dignified living conditions, often under the threat of losing their admission or career. I believe this story deserves wider attention, as it directly concerns the wellbeing, rights, and safety of the people who form the backbone of our healthcare system. I would be happy to share further documentation, photographs, or put you in touch with fellow students and junior doctors willing to speak on record or on condition of anonymity.

Please let me know if you would like to discuss this further or require any additional information.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Warm regards,

Sarthak Bhai, I genuinely want to understand your position here, because I feel there are some serious inconsistencies in the way you are looking at these protests.

First, please watch your own Jharkhand video, where you yourself acknowledged that thousands of people were coming and going, and in such a massive crowd, it is impossible to know exactly who was raising which slogan. If random slogans can be dismissed as the actions of individuals in one protest, then how can you use particular slogans in another protest to characterize the entire movement as organized or ideological? Isn’t that a double standard?

The comparison people in this de-reservation protest are making with CJP also needs to be understood properly. They are comparing themselves with CJP because, as they understand it, CJP had permission to conduct its protest at that particular place, whereas these protesters were not initially even given permission to protest there. Yes, permission was later granted for a protest at Ramlila Maidan, but that does not automatically make the original treatment of their protest fair.

And honestly, before judging any protest, I think we should actually read their demands and understand what they are asking for instead of simply labeling the entire movement.

One of the demands I personally find worth discussing is the idea that reservation should perhaps be given to a family only once, rather than continuing indefinitely across generations within the same family. Another version of the demand is that reservation should continue until someone from that family achieves a certain level of economic and social stability and moves above the genuinely disadvantaged category.

Whether we agree with this proposal or not, it deserves an actual discussion.

The same logic should apply when we talk about EWS. If EWS reservation is intended for economically weaker sections, then shouldn’t its benefits primarily reach people who are genuinely economically disadvantaged?

People also ask a very basic question: what about a genuinely poor person from a community that does not receive caste-based reservation? Has that person done something wrong simply because they were born into a particular community?

At the same time, if someone who is already financially well-off manages to obtain a fraudulent certificate and takes benefits intended for genuinely disadvantaged people, that is obviously a serious problem too.

I know these issues are not perfectly interconnected, but they are all part of the larger conversation about how reservation should work, who should qualify, and how we can ensure that benefits actually reach the people who need them.

I am not saying there is a simple answer to all of this. My point is that we should discuss reservation, protests, eligibility, economic disadvantage, misuse of certificates, representation and equality using the same standard for everyone.

And coming back to the original question: are you actually against reservation, or are you against certain aspects of the current reservation system? Because those are two very different positions.

And finally, let’s take the competence argument seriously. Suppose a student scores -40 marks in an examination and eventually becomes a doctor because of reservation. Would you personally be comfortable getting a major operation done by that person?

If the answer is no, then shouldn’t we honestly discuss where we draw the line between social justice, representation, economic disadvantage and professional competence?

The point isn’t to attack anyone. The point is to have a consistent conversation where the same standards are applied to everyone.

Reservation should be strictly based on economic criteria. The primary purpose of reservation should be the economic upliftment of socially and economically disadvantaged communities.
If a person from an SC/ST background benefits from reservation and becomes a government employee, their children should no longer automatically qualify for reservation. This would ensure that the benefits reach genuinely disadvantaged families and give economically weaker people more opportunities.

I think this is the best response to those asking why people don’t support the “Reservation Hatao” movement.
Reservation can be reformed, but it cannot simply be abolished. There is a huge scope for a rational debate on its implementation, eligibility criteria, benefits, exclusions, and how it should evolve with changing social and economic realities. That discussion is absolutely valid.
But demanding its complete removal while ignoring the historical and social inequalities that reservation was created to address is not a solution, it is an oversimplification.
And when the same people demanding “Reservation Hatao” proudly raise slogans like “Brahminism Zindabad” and “Baniyavad Zindabad,” the contradiction becomes obvious.
If you genuinely want to debate reservation, then let’s debate it with facts, constitutional values, equality, and social justice, not by glorifying caste-based hierarchies.

Reform the system. Debate the system. Improve the system. But don’t pretend that centuries of social inequality can be solved simply by deleting reservation.

Hello Bhaiya and everyone,
Here's what I feel about being in India and being categorised as Schedule Caste, I belong from Raipur, Chhattisgarh, recently we were looking for an apartment to rent while our home was renovated, the very first question which the landlords and landladies would ask was, "Aapki Jaati kya hoti hai, kisme aate hai aap?" Well I'm 22 now and used to such kind of questions, and the moment we said, Schedule Caste - Satnami, they would politely deny us from entering their property.
Another incident is that, I went to a really good school of Chhattisgarh, I mean top 2nd, their we were only 3 students from Sc,Stand Obc and rest all of them were from General category and the moment our class teacher announced that for the registration in the CBSE board examination of 12th Standard we require our Caste Certificate and mind you that announcements with our names that these 3 students need to bring their caste certificates made the entire class look at us like we are from some different planet and I felt like dying at that moment. I somehow belong to a good background where my father is an engineer because of reservation, but my grandfather was illiterate, my great grandfather was also illiterate and so on, where as there are my uppered class friends whose parents, grandparents, great grandparents were somehow very educated and had a well paid job. Coming to the other incident, when I visited my doc for my regular checkup he asked me, "Are you also a part of the drama going on at Jantar Mantar" I said yes, and then he said  "saare neele kabutar ikkathhe hai wahan", people talk about that creamy layer should be introduced in SC-Sts I just have one question, despite of belonging from a good and stable economic background I feel the discrimination. The moment I entered LSR with a reserved seat, people there made fun of me, also with the same reservation of EWS people don't have a problem...so I don't think in anywhich way castism has decreased or will be out of our society even in future because the way through which it was performed has changed but castism still exists.

There were 3 girls in the metro discussing how badly SC-STs stink and how dark their skin colour is?

Also a question to everyone who is reading this, I don't see a single millionaire from SC-Sts, I can't find the name tags of the banglows in south Delhi having the titles of SC-Sts, I can't find a general category sewage worker, I can't see any general category person cleaning that man hole for food. If people can have purity hawans after the visit of Kharge ji, if people can make fun of our Tribal President and who am I or the other SC-Sts personnel to not face castism.
Reservation gave my father education, reservation gave me a place at LSR, it gave me an opportunity, wealth does not always define your social dignity.

Bro, regarding what you're saying about the scam—one house being used for photos of 3,000 people—something similar happens in Bihar too.

For example, under the government toilet (Swachh Bharat) scheme in many villages, only one person actually builds a toilet. After that, people from the entire village stand in front of the same toilet one by one and get their photos clicked as if each of them has built one. The official who comes for verification often takes a cut. Suppose the government releases ₹10,000; the verifier may keep around ₹5,000 and give the remaining amount to the beneficiary.

So I don't think it's entirely a government scam. During audits, officials often don't verify the actual ground reality. The bigger issue is that many local people themselves don't want genuine development. Even today, in my village, many people still go to the roadside instead of using toilets, and they spend the government money on other personal needs.

The same thing happens with government housing schemes. The government allocates money for houses, but only one house gets built. Then people from the entire village use that same house for photos to claim benefits. Out of ₹100,000, the verification official may take ₹40,000–₹50,000, and the rest is shared.

This has been happening in many rural areas of Bihar. If possible, you should also cover this aspect on the ground. The government may be providing the funds, but if local people and corrupt officials misuse the schemes, real development never happens. Then, when the government doesn't provide benefits, people blame the government, and when it does, some people still don't want actual development and continue living in mud houses while misusing the funds.

I believe some police officers may have misused their authority. If any officer used excessive force or acted unlawfully, they should be investigated, suspended if necessary, and punished according to the law.

In that scenario, many police officers, protesters, or even innocent bystanders could have been seriously injured or even lost their lives.

I've also seen several videos showing some protesters provoking the police, throwing stones, or using pepper spray. I'm **not** saying every protester behaved this way, but these incidents should not be ignored either.

My view on the 20 July protest:

I believe some police officers may have misused their authority. If any officer used excessive force or acted unlawfully, they should be investigated, suspended if necessary, and punished according to the law.

At the same time, I do not support the decision to organize an unauthorized march toward Parliament. In my opinion, if such a large crowd had reached Parliament and the situation had gone completely out of control, the risk of a Red Fort 2021–type incident would have been very high. In that scenario, many police officers, protesters, or even innocent bystanders could have been seriously injured or even lost their lives.

I've also seen several videos showing some protesters provoking the police, throwing stones, or using pepper spray. I'm **not** saying every protester behaved this way, but these incidents should not be ignored either.

This is why I support neither police misconduct nor the way this protest was conducted. The students' concerns may be genuine, but there were legal and peaceful alternatives to demonstrate without marching toward Parliament.
